claims.text: A physics-informed multiscale surrogate model can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior for HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate model will reduce prediction error by approximately 10–20% relative to established full-scale atomistic simulations.
The surrogate model will be approximately 20–30% faster than established full-scale atomistic simulations.
As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 possesses a hierarchical heterostructure with a primary BCC matrix.
As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 contains well-distributed nanoscale secondary phases or precipitates.
The nanoscale secondary phases in HfNbTiVAl10 form distinct interfaces with the BCC matrix.
The proposed framework will encode phase boundaries, precipitate morphology, and precipitate volume fraction as mediators of elastic and plastic behavior.
The hierarchical heterostructure remains stable and statistically homogeneous during room-temperature tests at moderate strain rates.
Interfaces between the BCC matrix and nanoscale secondary phases govern load transfer in HfNbTiVAl10.
Interfaces between the BCC matrix and nanoscale secondary phases block dislocations in HfNbTiVAl10.
Interfaces between the BCC matrix and nanoscale secondary phases deflect cracks in HfNbTiVAl10.
Effective-medium approximations incorporating microstructural descriptors can capture how phase boundaries mediate the onset of plasticity.
Effective-medium approximations incorporating microstructural descriptors can capture how phase boundaries affect crack propagation.
Representing phase-boundary effects through microstructural descriptors removes the need for full atomistic resolution.
The surrogate model will predict the measured mechanical properties within ±10–20% of experimental values.
Established full-scale molecular-dynamics or atomistically informed finite-element simulations require significantly longer computation times.
Established simulations have prediction errors similar to or larger than those expected for the surrogate model.

The approach may fail at very high strain rates, at temperatures causing phase transformations, or in processing-inhomogeneous samples because the actual microstructure will deviate from the model inputs.
